title: An AI-native org isn't everyone using AI — it's assuming the org doesn't exist and rebuilding it
dek: Lockin merged HR and IT into HARO, put a technical founder-type in charge of people and AI; circle leads hold the bonus-pool allocation power, and hiring someone requires first proving AI can't do the job.
why: The founder of a 12-year hardware company explains the concrete mechanics of rewriting an organization: HARO, circles, AI management trainees, how FDEs actually land — with details and the pitfalls.
who: Founders pushing AI org transformation, HR leaders and business owners — especially at hardware or consumer electronics companies who want to move on org design but don't know where to start.
skip: After 1:04:25 the chit-chat and outro music can be skipped.

points.h: AI-native starts by assuming the organization doesn't exist
points.body: Chen Bin's definition of an AI-native organization is not ‘everyone should use AI well’ but rather starting from AI and asking again: can AI do this thing, and as far as possible don't let a person do it. The more brutal step is to assume the original organization and processes don't exist — ‘they shouldn't even exist’ — and go back to the state of a single founder starting a company to redesign roles and processes. So this is not accelerating existing processes; it's tearing the processes down first and rebuilding them. He admits this is mainly aimed at the core org builders, not a slogan shouted at everyone.

points.h: The HARO lead comes from tech, not HR
points.body: Lockin merged HR and IT into HARO (Human AI Resource Office), but Chen Bin stresses it is not an ordinary HR+IT combo: the lead must understand the business, and the person chosen is an old partner who started the company with him and has done technology, product, CEO, R&D, brand and IT. The logic is inverted — the old HR lead leaned toward people and was insensitive to AI, so now a tech-oriented person leads it, with HR BPs who are sensitive to people assigned to him. Under this department sit the AIO (the former IT team, which will do Agent Builder in future) on a solid line, and FDEs reporting on a dotted line.

points.h: Agent Builder and FDE are two kinds of people in the short term
points.body: Chen Bin draws the line clearly: Agent Builder leans technical, able to build an Agent; the FDE has to go into the business front line, sort out supply, planning and procurement processes, and is best a business expert. Long term one person might cover it; short term two kinds of people must work together. They did not copy Anker's approach of pulling people out of work and locking them away for a month, because they don't have that much slack; instead they let business people spend 30% to 50% of their energy doing AI-ification alongside their business work. The company also set up AI proficiency levels L1 to L4, with L2 and above called ‘AI 起航员’ (AI navigators), and above that ‘领航员’ (pilots).

points.h: Circles erase functional power; circle leads hold the bonus-pool allocation power
points.body: Lockin's circles differ from project teams and from Huawei's matrix: a matrix is product line plus function on two axes, while a circle is a small team with an end-to-end value loop, deliberately erasing functional power and boundaries so the circle lead's power grows. The company gives the circle a bonus pool, and the circle lead decides how to split it — even how much to give himself — while HR and functional departments only have an advisory voice. Chen Bin says at this stage the ‘fighting’ line dominates; the functional line may in future become something like a technology committee, but within the first six months to a year of the transformation the front line gets to decide.

points.h: Experience can become a burden instead
points.body: Chen Bin says AI management trainees naturally started using AI from university in 2023, have no fear of doing things, and use it more than the veterans. His exact words: ‘sometimes experience instead becomes a burden’, and the most troublesome are the half-baked — whose experience hasn't arrived but who feel they are very experienced and can't change. Veterans have framework thinking and systematic thinking as a foundation, but on which processes and which roles can be removed, the clear-eyed judge more easily. The threshold for AI management trainees is internal AI level L2 or above, requiring skill with skills and the ability to build Agents; only L3 can author workflows.

points.h: R&D turns fast, marketing turns slow
points.body: Chen Bin admits the speed of transformation varies a lot by department: technical R&D tied to software and coding is easiest, since writing code every day gives positive feedback; marketing and branding are slow, because after publishing more content they ask ‘so what’ — did it bring revenue growth and higher bonuses. He also mentions a real conflict: people doing design and content feel AI can only accelerate quantity, not raise quality, and that 60-point output doesn't stick. His response is to give everyone an operating mindset: whether content can drive conversion is the standard.

points.h: Three rounds of sign-ups: stand up again, then sit down again
points.body: Lockin ran three rounds of internal sign-ups: the first for incremental roles, such as the company-level ten or twenty Agents and the corresponding Agent Builders and FDEs; the second for roles missing after circles were formed, such as a content marketing Agent Builder; the third to keep filling gaps. Applicants first do a self-assessment to discover what they are good at, then give a three-to-five-minute defense, and after the judges score, AI is used to analyze the meeting minutes and the talk for matching. Of a hundred applicants, twenty or thirty may finally be chosen. Chen Bin says both the mechanism and the results are very good.

points.h: Hiring someone requires first proving AI can't do the job
points.body: After people from the original departments are picked by circles, when a boss wants to add headcount there are logically only two channels: find an AI management trainee, or use more AI tokens. If someone really must be hired again, it goes to Chen Bin for special approval, and he has to explain clearly why a management trainee can't be used and why AI can't be used. Chen Bin says ‘logically he has no channel left’. They plan to hire 50 AI management trainees by year-end, and are already close to 20. Xiaofei's role at Lockin is like a strategic HR, a CHO as a service, working with Chen Bin on the AI-native transformation.

points.h: IPD is not overturned, only accelerated
points.body: Chen Bin says inside the company he is actually the most radical one, and people often pull him back to be more cautious. On accumulations like Huawei's IPD, his judgment is: AI can only transform processes that were already unreasonable and especially redundant; IPD itself is very reasonable and can only be accelerated. For example, SP to BP, from strategy to execution, used to take three months to half a year, now two months, doubling efficiency, but the nodes like Five Looks Three Sets are still there — it's just that what took three weeks now takes three days. Training a product line manager used to take 10 to 15 years, now three to five years, but the rotation posts that should be rotated through cannot be skipped.

points.h: Not every company should run this fast
points.body: Chen Bin's advice to three kinds of bosses — milk tea shops, PCB factories, call centers — is to look at the real value AI brings in that industry: the more traditional the industry, the lower the value, and you can wait until platforms like Doubao and Volcano Engine mature before choosing, with lower trial-and-error cost. But the more frontier the tech company, the earlier it should embrace AI, because technology changes a lot and the market changes fast, and decision quality matters more. He specifically notes that before physical AI takes off, PCB factories and the like should be cautious and not move first; milk tea shops are more channel- and operations-driven, and AI can quickly build a feedback loop from the user end to the supply chain end, so its effect is greater.

quotes.text: I think an AI-native organization probably starts from AI first — whatever AI can do, try not to have a person do it. Think AI-native first, and think about this thing, even this process, as something that logically should be rebuilt.

It used to be functional, right? Now I'm an end-to-end small team with a value loop, and I even deliberately erase the functional power, or the boundaries — make the functional power smaller and the circle's power, or the circle lead's power, bigger.

Actually sometimes experience instead becomes a burden. It's better to have it, but the half-baked are the scary ones — their experience hasn't arrived yet, but they feel they're already very experienced, right? Can't change.

As far as possible we fill with AI, right? Prioritize using AI — whatever AI can fill, let AI fill it. Unless it can't be filled, and if it can't, then internally we say: either you say you'll find an AI management trainee to fill it, or you use more AI tokens.

It used to take at least three months to half a year; now we do SP to BP in two months, right? At least double the efficiency. But the process itself hasn't changed — it's just that where I used to hold five meetings, now I hold three, or two.

Actually look at the real value AI brings in that industry. I think the more traditional the industry, the lower the value it brings — lower, so you can reasonably say you can wait until these — like us, the ones who dig pits and play around, right? — or like Doubao at work, Volcano Engine, until those are done well, and then you just choose.
